methodological_rigor.justification: Secondary qualitative analysis of Canadian Transitions Survey with 399 respondents aged ≥85 years. Content analysis performed inductively by multiple investigators with consensus coding of open-ended responses. Chi-square tests for categorical comparisons across income/gender groups (p<0.05 significance). No quantitative outcome measures or effect size calculations. Significant limitations: very high non-response rates (59.6% blank on main challenges vs 35.7% overall cohort), only 17.8% provided improvement suggestions, no power calculations, no adjustment for multiple comparisons in descriptive analyses.

clinical_relevance_loe.justification: Descriptive case series (LoE 4) of cancer survivor experiences without comparative group or outcome measurements. Identifies unmet supportive care needs in underresearched ≥85-year-old population. Clinical relevance limited by lack of actionable interventions or evidence-based recommendations; findings primarily inform service development hypotheses.

reporting_quality.justification: Qualitative secondary analysis without standard reporting checklist (QUOROM/COREQ). Methods describe coding framework and chi-square comparisons but lack rigor of qualitative reporting: no audit trail, limited reflexivity on investigator bias, brief narrative responses difficult to interpret without follow-up interviews. Authors acknowledge brief written responses posed challenge. Data availability: housed in publicly available platform but limited raw data sharing described.

novelty_literature.justification: First Canadian study examining cancer survivor concerns ≥85 years stratified by gender and income. Identifies physical challenges (bladder/bowel 12.5%, mobility 12.9%, fatigue 11.4%), emotional concerns (fear of recurrence 35.7%), service gaps as primary themes. Findings largely confirmatory of known survivor needs without novel insights specific to oldest-old population.

writing_presentation.justification: Clearly organized qualitative paper with transparent acknowledgment of methodological limitations including high non-response rates (59.6% vs 35.7% overall), lack of detailed written responses, survey completion barriers in oldest-old. Discussion thoughtfully addresses potential mechanisms for non-response (sensory deficits, cognitive challenges, fatigue). However, interpretations somewhat speculative given sparse data.

key_strengths: Addresses important gap in understanding needs of rapidly growing ≥85-year-old cancer survivor population, currently double the representation in sample vs Canadian population (4.67% vs 2.3%)

Transparent acknowledgment of significant methodological constraints including very high non-response rates (59.6% on main challenges), brief narratives limiting interpretation, and likely under-representation of most vulnerable survivors
Multi-investigator coding with consensus discussion enhances rigor of qualitative content analysis; data housed in publicly available Canadian Partnership Against Cancer platform

Identifies important intersectionality factors: marital status (71.6% married men vs 21.8% married women) and income level (73.6% under $50K vs 51.1% Canadian population) potentially influencing supportive care needs
key_concerns: Extremely high non-response rate (59.6% blank/no response on main challenges vs 35.7% for all survey respondents, 82.2% no suggestions vs 21.5%) suggests substantial selection bias and possible exclusion of most vulnerable or least engaged survivors

Qualitative data too sparse for robust analysis: brief written responses without follow-up interviews limit interpretability; only 17.8% of respondents provided improvement suggestions; content analysis limited by inability to probe or seek clarification

No quantitative outcome measures; chi-square comparisons underpowered given small subgroup sizes; no adjustment for multiple comparisons despite numerous statistical tests; findings described as 'raising questions' rather than establishing evidence

Respondents aged ≥85 years under-represented in original survey (4.67% of respondents vs ~18% of Canadians ≥85 diagnosed with cancer); heterogeneity across 10 provincial health systems limits interpretability and generalizability
chief_reviewer.rationale: Exploratory qualitative secondary analysis addressing important gap in ≥85-year-old cancer survivor research, but severe methodological limitations including very high non-response rates, sparse qualitative data, and lack of quantitative rigor limit tier to 4. Appropriate for specialty journals as hypothesis-generating work requiring future prospective qualitative interviews.
